Market Updates

blocks.html: Over the last quarter, the global macroeconomic and aviation landscape was shaped, to some extent, by the outbreak of armed conflict in the Middle East beginning in late February 2026. Below we have summarized where we believe the aviation industry stands as of Q1 2026.
blocks.text: Over the last quarter, the global macroeconomic and aviation landscape was shaped, to some extent, by the outbreak of armed conflict in the Middle East beginning in late February 2026. Below we have summarized where we believe the aviation industry stands as of Q1 2026.

items: Middle East Conflict & Fuel Prices: US-Israeli strikes on Iranian oil infrastructure in late February sent jet fuel prices up approximately 63% in one month, rising to $3.70 per gallon in March from $2.26 pre-conflict.1 Unlike COVID-19, this is a cost and network shock rather than a demand collapse leaving passenger appetite to remain intact. A ceasefire was announced in late April, and we continue to monitor developments, though we note the Fund's asset-backed, long-term lease structure provides meaningful insulation from near-term fuel price volatility.

Airline Profitability: Airlines entered 2026 on strong footing, with IATA projecting a record $41Bn in net profit at a 3.9% net margin, supported by robust demand and record-high load factors.2 While the fuel spike introduces near-term margin pressure, stronger carriers are better positioned to absorb costs through fare increases and surcharges. It is precisely these well positioned counterparties that anchor the Fund's lessee base.

Supply / Demand: The global order backlog has surpassed 17,000 aircraft, nearly 60% of the active fleet and equivalent to nearly 12 years of current production capacity.2 The conflict has only deepened this imbalance: supply chain disruptions are further delaying fleet renewal, airspace rerouting is increasing the number of aircraft airlines need to maintain schedules, and the window during which carriers must rely on leased in-service aircraft continues to extend – all of which are dynamics that we believe benefit our strategy.

blocks.text: Aircraft Fund & Business Update

items: Since the Fund's initial closing in April 2025, we have secured over $350M of capital commitments3. We are actively advancing discussions with a number of prospective investors and expect additional closings over the next several months, ahead of a targeted final close in October.

From an investment standpoint, the Fund has committed to acquire 33x aircraft and 5x engine assets, representing ~$1.1Bn of asset value. These transactions have been originated at what we believe are attractive entry points, underwriting to returns in line with our mid-teens net target.

During Q1 2026, the Fund committed to two transactions that we believe meaningfully strengthen the portfolio. The first is the acquisition of 6x new-technology 737 MAX 8 aircraft, scheduled to begin delivering in Q3 2026, adding high-quality narrowbody assets at attractive entry points. The second is the acquisition of a 14x aircraft portfolio executed as a portfolio sale – a structure our team was well positioned to underwrite, which we believe facilitated timely execution and a clear path to integration into our Master Trust. Together, these transactions broaden the Fund's diversification across lessees, geographies, and asset types, while we believe it should improve the overall return profile of the pro forma portfolio.

In March 2026, the Fund executed the monetization of one 737-9 aircraft on lease to United Airlines in the Japanese tax equity market. We have a second aircraft on lease to United under a contractual agreement to close in the same market and anticipate a near-term closing.

Through Q1 2026, the Fund is tracking above our high-single-digit distributable cash yield target. Capital called to date represents 16% of equity commitments and we anticipate an additional 8–10% of capital to be called over the next two quarters, though this reflects our current view and may evolve as the pipeline develops. We are actively evaluating several investments for the Fund and remain committed to growing the portfolio with discipline.

blocks.html: PERFORMANCE CALCULATIONS METHODOLOGIES 1. Multiple of Money (MoM) is equal to the total value for each investment divided by the investment amount for such investment. 2. Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is a measure of the discounted cash flows (inflows and outflows) related to an investment. Specifically, IRR is the discount rate at which the net present value of all cash flows and any remaining investment value is equal to zero. In other words, IRR is the discount rate at which the (i) present value of all capital invested in an investment (including expenses specifically allocable to the investment) is equal to (ii) the present value of all returns from the investment (whether or not realized). 3. Net IRR (To Date) reflects the impact of management fees, fund expenses and carried interest or incentive fee allocations that have been allocated to limited partners. 4. In certain vehicles Bain Capital Special Situations has deferred portions of carried interest accrual to the General Partner as contemplated within the applicable vehicle’s legal documents. During the deferral period, accrued carried interest is not reallocated from the limited partners’ book capital accounts to the account of the General Partner. 5. IRRs shown include all returns generated by reinvested capital and profit. 6. Annualized returns are computed based on the change in value during the period of a theoretical investment made at the beginning of the period. The change in value of a theoretical investment is measured by comparing the aggregate ending value of Limited Partners with the aggregate beginning value adjusted for cash flows related to capital contributions or withdrawals during the period. Returns are geometrically linked on a monthly basis. 7. Fund-level gross and net IRRs are calculated based on the timing and values of cash flows from limited partners. The methodology used for calculating the fund-level gross and net IRR is consistent. 8. The Partnerships or accounts may utilize credit facilities, which are secured by unfunded investor commitments or asset value, to facilitate funding needs. The use of the Partnership's one or more credit facilities may impact the timing of cash flows reflected in IRR calculations, and thereby impact the IRRs presented herein. Differences in IRRs will depend on a number of factors including the amount borrowed by the Partnership, the timing of repayments of the credit facilities, as well as the applicable interest amounts under the credit facilities.

blocks.html: The Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 Portfolios are distinct groups of aircrafts owned by the Bain Capital and Griffin Global Asset Management platform. Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 are owned by different Bain Capital Special Situations’ Funds though all aircraft across Vintages are held within a corporate entity where any related financing is comingled, i.e. the Bain Capital / Griffin Platform. Further details on the portfolio are noted below. 1. Vintage 1: The portfolio’s first aircraft was acquired on January 7, 2021 and is owned primarily by the Global Special Situations I and Special Situations Asia I. As of December 31, 2024, the Vintage 1 portfolio owns 34 delivered aircraft. 2. Vintage 2: The portfolio’s first aircraft was acquired on September 23, 2022 and is owned primarily by the Global Special Situations II and Special Situations Asia II. As of December 31, 2024, the Vintage 2 portfolio owns 31 delivered aircraft and 27 engines. 3. Combined returns for Vintage 1 and Vintage 2 are extracted performance across multiple funds and may be deemed to be “hypothetical” performance. Hypothetical performance is subject to inherent limitations, as the performance may have been different had the investments been selected to occur in one fund. 4. Net returns were calculated using the following assumptions and in line with the undiscounted Aircraft Fund fees and expenses reflected in the offering documents: a) Management fees are based on the weighted average life of the investments multiplied by the total invested capital multiplied by 1.50%. b) Carried interest percentage is 20% c) Operating expenses are based on the weighted average life of the investments multiplied by the total invested capital multiplied by 0.25%
